Summary: The fourth commandment: one day in seven is set apart for rest and worship, rooted in creation and in Israel's deliverance from Egypt.
Commandment: Keep one day in seven holy: rest from ordinary work and set it apart for God.
Application: Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath and teaches that the Sabbath was made for people, not people for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28). Christians differ on whether seventh-day observance continues literally or is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9-10); both readings are honestly held.
Purpose: Scripture gives two stated grounds: creation rest (Exodus 20:11) and deliverance from Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). Debated: some Christians keep a seventh-day Sabbath literally; others see the Sabbath fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (Hebrews 4:9-10). The site does not settle this.
Function: One day in seven, set apart — this fourth of the Ten Words is foundational moral law in the traditional classification, though its exact observance is debated among Christians and this entry does not settle it. Its goal was rest and worship rooted in two grounds Scripture itself gives: creation rest and deliverance from Egypt. The evil it addressed was a life with no stopping — work without end, God crowded out. It restrained that evil by fencing one day off: ordinary work stops, and the day belongs to God.
